title: Implementing tools
summary: Tool use lets Claude call tools that your application executes (client tools, including Anthropic-schema ones like `bash`) or that Anthropic runs (server tools). You describe each tool you define with a name, a detailed description and an `input_schema`; for client tools, your code runs each call and returns a `tool_result`. The description is by far the most important factor in tool performance.
keyPoints: Descriptions matter most: what the tool does, when to use it (and when not), each parameter, caveats. Aim for **at least 3–4 sentences**.
`tool_choice`: **auto** (default with tools), **any**, **tool**, **none**. Opus 5.5, Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1 return a 400 for `any` and `tool`.
Parallel calls: return **every** `tool_result` in **one** user message, with results before any text.
Set `is_error: true` for a failed or skipped call, with an instructive message on what to try next.
Client tools (yours, and Anthropic-schema ones like `bash`) run in your app; server tools (like `web_search`) run on Anthropic's infrastructure.

sections.heading: Defining a tool
sections.body:
A user-defined tool in the `tools` parameter has a `name` (matching `^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]{1,128}$`), a `description` and an `input_schema`, a JSON Schema object. The API builds a special system prompt from your tool definitions.

Anthropic's best practices:

- Provide extremely detailed descriptions: what the tool does, when to use it (and when not), what each parameter means, and caveats
- For complex or format-sensitive inputs, add `input_examples`; each must be valid against the schema, or the request returns a 400
- Consolidate related operations into fewer tools, such as one tool with an `action` parameter
- Prefix names with the service, like `github_list_prs`
- Return only high-signal information, with stable identifiers

sections.heading: Controlling when tools are called
sections.body:
With the default `tool_choice` of `auto`, Claude decides whether to call a tool. `any` requires one of your tools, `tool` forces a named tool, and `none` prevents tool use. With `any` or `tool`, the API prefills the assistant message, so Claude won't write text before the `tool_use` block.

Forced tool use isn't always available. Manual extended thinking doesn't support `any` or `tool`, and on Claude Opus 5.5, Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1 they return a 400 error. There, use `auto` with strict tool use (`strict: true`) for schema-valid inputs, or structured outputs for a response in a fixed JSON shape.

sections.heading: Running the loop
sections.body:
For client tools, your application drives a loop: send the request, get `stop_reason: "tool_use"`, run each tool, send the results back in a user message, and repeat while `stop_reason` is `"tool_use"`. Server tools run their own loop on Anthropic's infrastructure, and you read the results.

When Claude returns several `tool_use` blocks, you choose the execution order. Independent, read-only calls are usually safe to run in parallel; calls with side effects or ordering requirements might be better run sequentially. Either way, send one `tool_result` per call, all in one user message, before any text. Set `is_error: true` for a failure or a call you skipped, and say what went wrong and what to try next.

The SDK tool runner automates this loop. When you need human-in-the-loop approval, custom logging or conditional execution, write the manual loop instead.

title: Building and connecting MCP servers
summary: An MCP server exposes tools, resources and prompts to AI applications over a transport: stdio for a local process, or Streamable HTTP for a remote server. You build one with an MCP SDK, then connect it to a host such as Claude Code, or to the Messages API through the MCP connector.
keyPoints: Building blocks: **tools** (model-controlled), **resources** (application-driven), **prompts** (user-controlled).
**stdio**: local, typically one client. **Streamable HTTP**: remote, typically many clients, standard HTTP auth (MCP recommends OAuth).
In a stdio server, **never write to stdout**: it corrupts the JSON-RPC messages. Log to stderr.
The MCP connector needs a **publicly exposed HTTP** server and currently supports only **tool calls**.
Claude Code: `claude mcp add --transport http <name> <url>` for remote servers; a stdio server's command goes after `--`.

sections.heading: What a server offers
sections.body:
MCP follows a client-server architecture: a host such as Claude Code or Claude Desktop creates one MCP client for each server it connects to. Servers provide three building blocks:

- Tools: functions the model can call to perform actions
- Resources: passive, read-only data for context, each with a unique URI
- Prompts: reusable templates the user invokes explicitly, for example as slash commands

Clients discover each kind with `*/list` methods, which lets the listings be dynamic.

sections.heading: Choosing a transport
sections.body:
Both transports carry the same JSON-RPC 2.0 messages.

- stdio: the client launches the server as a subprocess, and they talk over standard input and output on the same machine, with no network overhead
- Streamable HTTP: HTTP POST for client-to-server messages, with optional Server-Sent Events for streaming; it enables remote servers and standard HTTP authentication

In a stdio server, never write logs to stdout: `print()` in Python or `console.log()` in TypeScript corrupts the JSON-RPC messages. Write to stderr instead. For HTTP-based servers, stdout logging is fine.

A Streamable HTTP server must validate the `Origin` header, and when running locally it should bind only to localhost (127.0.0.1), to prevent DNS rebinding attacks.

diagram.caption: From SDK to a connected server.

sections.heading: Connecting servers to Claude
sections.body:
In Claude Code, HTTP servers are the recommended option for remote servers, and the SSE transport is deprecated: `claude mcp add --transport http <name> <url>`. A local stdio server takes its launch command after `--`, as in `claude mcp add --transport stdio myserver -- npx server`.

From the Messages API, the MCP connector (beta) connects to remote servers without a separate MCP client. Define each server in `mcp_servers`, with a URL that starts with https, and reference it from exactly one `mcp_toolset` in `tools`, where you can allowlist or denylist tools. Only tool calls are currently supported, and local stdio servers can't be connected directly.

sources.title: Connect Claude Code to tools via MCP

title: Customising agents with skills, subagents, MCP and plugins
summary: Claude Code's built-in tools cover most coding tasks; extensions customise what Claude knows, connect it to external services and automate workflows. Skills add on-demand knowledge, subagents isolate work, MCP connects external systems, and plugins package them. Review third-party skills, MCP servers and plugins before you trust them.
keyPoints: Skills use **progressive disclosure**: metadata (~100 tokens each) always, the SKILL.md body when triggered, files and script output as needed.
A Skill's `description` must say what it does **and** when to use it; Claude matches requests against it.
Skill: reusable content in your context. **Subagent**: isolated worker that returns a summary. **MCP**: external services. **Plugin**: packaging.
In Claude Code, MCP tool search is on by default: tool names load at start, full schemas when needed.
A plugin can run code with **your user privileges**; hooks and MCP servers run outside the sandbox.

sections.heading: Match the feature to the goal
sections.body:
Claude Code combines the model with built-in tools for file operations, search, execution and web access, which cover most coding tasks. Extensions plug into different parts of the agentic loop:

- CLAUDE.md: persistent context loaded every session
- Skills: reusable knowledge and invocable workflows, loaded on demand
- MCP: connections to external services and data
- Subagents: isolated context that returns a summary
- Hooks: actions that run on lifecycle events
- Plugins: skills, subagents, hooks and MCP servers packaged as one installable unit

They combine. MCP can provide the database connection while a skill documents your schema and query patterns. Route a side task that floods your conversation through a subagent. For a skill with side effects, set `disable-model-invocation: true` so only you trigger it.

sections.heading: Agent Skills and progressive disclosure
sections.body:
A Skill is a directory with a `SKILL.md` file: YAML frontmatter (`name` and `description` are required) plus instructions, with optional scripts and reference files. Skills load in stages:

- Level 1, metadata: always loaded, about 100 tokens per Skill
- Level 2, the SKILL.md body: loaded when a request matches the description, under 5k tokens
- Level 3, bundled files: read only as needed; scripts run through bash, and only their output enters context

So you can install many Skills without context penalty. On the Claude API, Skills require the code execution tool; in Claude Code, put them in `~/.claude/skills/` or `.claude/skills/`.

diagram.caption: Each level loads only when it's needed.

sections.heading: Trusting third-party extensions
sections.body:
Use Skills only from trusted sources. A malicious Skill can direct Claude to invoke tools or execute code in ways that don't match its stated purpose, so audit every bundled file first. Verify you trust each MCP server before connecting it: servers that fetch external content can expose you to prompt injection.

A plugin you install can execute arbitrary code with your user privileges, whichever marketplace it comes from. Permission rules and the sandbox cover Claude's tool calls, not code the plugin runs by itself: hooks and MCP servers run outside the sandbox. Before installing, read `hooks/hooks.json`, `.mcp.json` and every file in `bin/`.

sources.title: Connect Claude Code to tools via MCP

title: The tool-use loop
summary: Tool use is a contract: you describe the tools, Claude decides when to call them, and your code runs each call. For client tools that means a loop of round trips keyed on `stop_reason`, built from four block types: `text`, `tool_use`, `tool_result` and `thinking`.
keyPoints: Six steps: **define schema → send message → `tool_use` block → execute tool → return `tool_result` → Claude continues**.
Keep looping while `stop_reason` is **`"tool_use"`**; any other stop reason (`end_turn`, `max_tokens`, …) exits the loop.
Claude writes `text`, `tool_use` and `thinking` blocks in the **assistant** message; you write `tool_result` blocks in the next **user** message.
`tool_result` blocks go **first** in that user message and carry the matching `tool_use_id`; text before them is a 400 error.
With thinking on, pass every `thinking` block back **complete and unmodified** alongside its `tool_use` block.

sections.heading: The loop in six steps
sections.body:
The **tool-use loop** is the round trip your application drives whenever Claude calls a client tool. The model never executes anything on its own: it emits a structured request, your code runs the operation, and the result flows back into the conversation.

- **Define schema:** describe each tool (name, description, `input_schema`) in the `tools` array.
- **Send message:** send the request with your tools and the user message.
- **`tool_use` block:** Claude responds with `stop_reason: "tool_use"` and one or more `tool_use` blocks.
- **Execute tool:** your code runs each call with the given input.
- **Return result:** send a new request with the original messages, Claude's response, and a user message holding the `tool_result` blocks.
- **Claude continues:** it uses the results to keep working, calling more tools or answering.
sections.example: A user asks "What's the weather in San Francisco?". Claude replies with a `tool_use` block: name `get_weather`, input `{"location": "San Francisco, CA"}`. Your code looks up the weather and sends back a `tool_result` with `"15 degrees Celsius, partly cloudy"`. Claude answers: "The current weather in San Francisco is 15 degrees Celsius with partly cloudy skies."

diagram.caption: Steps 3 to 6 repeat until Claude stops asking for tools.

sections.heading: stop_reason drives the loop
sections.body:
**`stop_reason`** tells you why Claude stopped. The canonical loop is a `while` loop keyed on it: while `stop_reason == "tool_use"`, execute the tools and continue the conversation.

The loop exits on any other stop reason (`"end_turn"`, `"max_tokens"`, `"stop_sequence"` or `"refusal"`), which means Claude has produced a final answer or stopped for another reason your application should handle.

Server tools such as `web_search` are different: Anthropic runs them in a server-side loop, so you never build a `tool_result` for them. If that loop hits its iteration limit, the response comes back with `stop_reason: "pause_turn"`, and you re-send the conversation to let Claude continue.
sections.example: Turn 1: `stop_reason: "tool_use"` → run `get_weather`, send the result. Turn 2: `stop_reason: "tool_use"` again (Claude now wants `get_time`) → run it, send the result. Turn 3: `stop_reason: "end_turn"` → the loop exits and you show Claude's text answer.

sections.heading: The four block types
sections.body:
A **content block** is one typed piece of a message's `content` array. Tool use is built into the normal `user` and `assistant` messages rather than a special `tool` role:

- **`text`** (Claude, assistant message): natural language, often a short comment on what Claude is about to do before it calls a tool. Treat it like any other assistant text; don't rely on its exact wording.
- **`tool_use`** (Claude, assistant message): a tool call with an `id`, the tool `name` and an `input` object matching the tool's `input_schema`.
- **`tool_result`** (your app, next user message): the output of one call, with `tool_use_id`, optional `content` and optional `is_error`.
- **`thinking`** (Claude, assistant message, when thinking is on): Claude's reasoning, arriving before the text or tool call, with a `signature` field you pass back unchanged.
sections.example:
Assistant: `[{"type": "text", "text": "I'll check the weather."}, {"type": "tool_use", "id": "toolu_01A", "name": "get_weather", "input": {"location": "San Francisco, CA"}}]`
User: `[{"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": "toolu_01A", "content": "15 degrees"}]`

sections.heading: Returning results without a 400
sections.body:
A **`tool_result`** answers one `tool_use` block. The formatting rules are strict:

- Tool results must immediately follow their tool use blocks: no other messages in between.
- In the user message, every `tool_result` block comes first; any text comes after all results.
- Each result names its call with `tool_use_id`. If Claude made several calls, return one result per call, all together in the next user message.

If the tool fails, still return a `tool_result`: put an instructive error message in `content` and set `"is_error": true`, and Claude incorporates the error into its response or retries.
sections.example: Before (400 error): a user message with a text block "Here are the results:" followed by the `tool_result`. After (works): the `tool_result` first, then the text block "What should I do next?".

sections.heading: Thinking blocks ride along
sections.body:
A **thinking block** holds Claude's reasoning when thinking is active. During tool use, Claude pauses its response to wait for your result, then continues building that same response, so its earlier reasoning must still be there.

When you send tool results back, pass every `thinking` block from that assistant message back to the API complete and unmodified, alongside the `tool_use` block it accompanied. Inside the latest assistant message you can't rearrange, edit or partially drop them.

A tool-use loop is one assistant turn, so the whole loop runs in a single thinking mode. Toggling thinking mid-turn doesn't error; the API silently disables thinking for that request. Change thinking settings between turns instead.
sections.example: Assistant: `[thinking] + [tool_use: get_weather]` → User: `[tool_result: "20°C, sunny"]` → Assistant: `[text: "The weather in Paris is 20°C and sunny"]`. The follow-up request must include the original `thinking` block, signature intact, in the assistant message.

title: Tool schemas Claude selects correctly
summary: Claude picks a tool and fills its inputs from three things you write: the name, the description and the `input_schema`. Of these, the description is by far the most important factor in tool performance, so when Claude picks the wrong tool, look at the schema, and above all the description, first.
keyPoints: A tool definition is a **name** (`^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]{1,128}$`), a detailed **description** and an **`input_schema`** (JSON Schema).
Detailed descriptions are **by far the most important factor**: what the tool does, when to use it (and not), each parameter, caveats. Aim for **3–4+ sentences**.
Chained steps that always run together can become **one tool** (`schedule_event`); only independent calls belong in a parallel batch.
Fields in `required` must be filled; if the user didn't supply one, Claude may ask (Opus, much more likely) or guess (Sonnet, sometimes).
Overlapping tools and vague parameter names confuse selection: **namespace** names (`asana_search`, `jira_search`) and use `user_id`, not `user`.

sections.heading: Schema anatomy: what Claude reads
sections.body:
A **tool definition** is what Claude reads to decide whether to call a tool and how. A user-defined tool has three core fields:

- **`name`**: must match `^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]{1,128}$`.
- **`description`**: a detailed plaintext description of what the tool does, when it should be used, and how it behaves.
- **`input_schema`**: a JSON Schema object for the parameters: their types, their own descriptions, and which are `required`.

When you send `tools`, the API builds a special system prompt from your tool definitions. Claude never sees your implementation; it only sees the schema you provided and the result you return. Claude determines when to call a tool based on the user's request and the tool's description.
sections.example: `{"name": "get_weather", "description": "Get the current weather in a given location", "input_schema": {"type": "object", "properties": {"location": {"type": "string", "description": "The city and state, e.g. San Francisco, CA"}, "unit": {"type": "string", "enum": ["celsius", "fahrenheit"]}}, "required": ["location"]}}`: `location` is required, `unit` is optional.

sections.heading: Decision table: schema design choices
sections.body:
Each schema design choice maps to a rule:

- **Subtask dependency:** steps that are always chained can become one tool that does the whole job; separate calls that depend on each other should run in order.
- **Required fields:** Claude must supply every field in `required`; if the user didn't give one, it may ask or infer a value.
- **Optional fields:** leave them out of `required` and describe what each one means and how it affects the tool's behavior; `input_examples` can show when to include them.
- **Description length:** at least 3–4 sentences per tool, more if it's complex. This is the biggest lever on selection.
- **Overlapping parameter types or tools:** give each tool a distinct purpose, namespace names by service or resource, and name inputs unambiguously (`user_id`, not `user`).

sections.heading: Subtask dependency: one tool or several?
sections.body:
**Subtask dependency** means one step needs another step's output. Anthropic recommends a few thoughtful tools for high-impact workflows rather than wrapping every API endpoint. A tool can consolidate several discrete operations and handle frequently chained, multi-step tasks in a single call, which also saves the context that intermediate outputs would have used.

You can also group related actions into one tool with an `action` parameter (`create_pr`, `review_pr`, `merge_pr` → one tool): fewer, more capable tools reduce selection ambiguity.

When you do keep separate tools, Claude can call several in one response. Independent, read-only calls are usually safe to run in parallel; calls with side effects or ordering requirements might be better run sequentially. A system-prompt line such as "Only batch tool calls that are independent of each other." reduces dependent calls appearing together.
sections.example: Instead of `list_users`, `list_events` and `create_event` (three chained calls), build `schedule_event`, which finds availability and schedules the event. Instead of `get_customer_by_id`, `list_transactions` and `list_notes`, build `get_customer_context`.

diagram.caption: Three always-chained calls become one tool call.

sections.heading: Required and optional fields
sections.body:
**Required fields** are listed in the schema's `required` array; **optional fields** are defined in `properties` but left out of it.

If the user's prompt doesn't include enough information to fill every required parameter, Claude Opus is much more likely to recognise the gap and ask. Claude Sonnet might ask, especially when prompted to think first, but it might also infer a reasonable value. This isn't guaranteed either way.

If Claude's tool call is invalid (for example, a required parameter is missing), it usually means it lacked the information to use the tool correctly: try more detailed descriptions first. `strict: true` guarantees inputs match your schema exactly. For complex or format-sensitive inputs, `input_examples` shows Claude when to include optional parameters; each example must be valid against `input_schema`, or the request returns a 400.
sections.example: "What's the weather?" with no city: Claude Sonnet might call `get_weather` with `{"location": "New York, NY", "unit": "fahrenheit"}`, guessing values you never supplied.

sections.heading: When Claude picks the wrong tool
sections.body:
When Claude picks the wrong tool, check the schema first, and the description before anything else: Anthropic calls detailed descriptions by far the most important factor in tool performance. Write descriptions the way you'd explain the tool to a new hire, making implicit context explicit. Even small refinements to tool descriptions can yield dramatic improvements.

Two more schema problems cause wrong picks:

- **Overlapping tools:** when tools overlap in function or have a vague purpose, agents can get confused about which one to use. Give each tool a distinct purpose and namespace names by service (`asana_search`, `jira_search`) or resource (`asana_projects_search`).
- **Ambiguous parameters:** name inputs unambiguously, `user_id` rather than `user`.
sections.example: Before: `search_orders` and `search_tickets` both say "Searches records." Asked "Is my refund ticket resolved?", Claude calls `search_orders`. After: `search_tickets` says it searches support tickets by customer or ticket ID, should be used for questions about support requests and refunds in progress, and does not return order or payment data. `search_orders` says the reverse, so Claude can now tell the two apart.

sources.title: Writing effective tools for agents — with agents

title: MCP vs writing schemas yourself
summary: When someone has already built the tools you need as an MCP server, you can connect to it instead of writing schemas and handlers yourself. The server supplies each tool's name, description and input schema, and runs the calls; the tool-use loop stays the same. Its descriptions steer Claude's choice just as much as yours do.
keyPoints: **MCP** is an open standard for connecting AI applications to external systems; servers expose **tools**, resources and prompts.
The client discovers tools with **`tools/list`** (name, description, `inputSchema`) and runs them with **`tools/call`**.
In the loop, the app hands MCP tools to Claude as tool definitions, routes each call to the right server, and returns the result to Claude.
Use MCP for services that already have a server; write schemas for **custom business logic, internal APIs, proprietary data**; mix both when you need both.
Claude selects MCP tools by **names and descriptions**: a vague server description sends Claude to the wrong tool just like a vague one of yours.

sections.heading: MCP: tools someone else already wrote
sections.body:
The **Model Context Protocol (MCP)** is an open-source standard for connecting AI applications to external systems. An **MCP server** exposes tools (executable functions), resources (data) and prompts (templates); the AI application, the **MCP host**, creates one **MCP client** per server it connects to.

For tool use this is the alternative to writing schemas by hand. A server's tool list already carries each tool's `name`, a `description` of what it does and when to use it, and an `inputSchema` (JSON Schema). With MCP, an agent can query databases and integrate with APIs like Slack and GitHub without writing custom tool implementations.
sections.example: A server's `tools/list` response includes `{"name": "weather_current", "title": "Weather Information", "description": "Get current weather information for any location worldwide", "inputSchema": {…, "required": ["location"]}}`: the same three things you'd otherwise write in a tool definition.

sections.heading: How MCP fits into the tool-use loop
sections.body:
MCP doesn't replace the tool-use loop; it changes who supplies the schemas and who runs the code:

- **Discover:** each MCP client sends `tools/list`; the application combines the tools from all connected servers into one registry the model can access.
- **Offer:** the application passes those tools to Claude as tool definitions.
- **Call:** Claude decides to use one and returns a tool call.
- **Route and run:** the application routes the call to the right server with `tools/call`.
- **Return:** it sends the server's result back to Claude as part of the conversation, and Claude continues.

On the Messages API, the **MCP connector** does the client side for you: list servers in `mcp_servers`, enable them with an `mcp_toolset` in `tools`, and the response shows `mcp_tool_use` and `mcp_tool_result` blocks. It currently supports only tool calls, and the server must be publicly exposed over HTTP.
sections.example: Python SDK pattern from the MCP docs: `for client in app.mcp_clients(): available_tools.extend((await client.list_tools()).tools)`, then on each tool call: `client = app.find_mcp_client_for_tool(tool_name)`; `result = await client.call_tool(tool_name, arguments)`; `conversation.add_tool_result(result.content)`.

diagram.caption: The loop is unchanged; the MCP server supplies the schemas and runs the calls.

sections.heading: Use MCP, write schemas, or use both
sections.body:
- **Use MCP when** a server already exists for the service (GitHub, Slack, Sentry, a database). You skip writing tool implementations, and because many clients support MCP, an integration can be built once and used across them.
- **Write schemas manually when** the tool is custom business logic, an internal API or proprietary data that lives in your application: you write the schema, run the code and return the result.
- **Use both when** an agent needs third-party services and your own logic. In the Agent SDK, connect external servers in `mcpServers` and define your own tools in code as an in-process SDK MCP server.

Pick the integration path by what you need: the MCP connector for remote servers reachable by URL when you only need tools; your own MCP client with the SDK's client-side MCP helpers (which convert MCP tools to Claude API tools) for local stdio servers, prompts, resources or more control.
sections.example: A support agent connects the remote GitHub MCP server (`mcpServers: {github: {type: "http", url: …}}`) for issues, and adds an in-process SDK MCP server for its own `issue_refund` logic. `allowedTools: ["mcp__github__list_issues", …]` auto-approves just the tools it needs.

sections.heading: The description that sent Claude to the wrong tool
sections.body:
MCP tools are selected exactly like your own: Claude calls an MCP tool when the user's request maps to the tool's **described capability**. With many tools available, Claude selects based on tool names and descriptions, and clear, specific descriptions improve selection accuracy.

So a server's description can send Claude to the wrong tool. When you connect many servers, tools from different developers can overlap in function or have vague purposes, and agents get confused about which to use. If you own the server, fix the description and name there (namespacing by service, such as `asana_search` vs `jira_search`, helps). For large tool sets (dozens of tools across several servers), `defer_loading` with the tool search tool surfaces only the relevant tools per query.
sections.example: Two connected servers each expose a tool described as "Search for items." Asked about a sprint task, Claude searches the wrong system. The fix: rename them `jira_search` and `asana_search`, and describe what each one searches and when to use it.

title: Durable project context
summary: Each Claude Code session starts with a fresh context window, so what Claude should always know needs a durable home. CLAUDE.md holds what every session needs, path-scoped rules hold guidance for one part of the codebase, hooks enforce what must happen every time, and subagents keep side work out of your context. Durable context means the right mechanism for each concern.
keyPoints: **CLAUDE.md** loads into every session as context, not enforced configuration. `/init` drafts a starter; review it and keep lines whose removal would cause mistakes.
Target **under 200 lines**. Move multi-step procedures and occasional reference material into **skills**, which load on demand; `@path` imports don't cut context.
A `.claude/rules/` file with **`paths`** frontmatter loads only when Claude reads, writes or edits a matching file; without `paths` it loads every session.
Hooks run at fixed lifecycle points. A **PreToolUse** deny blocks the call in every permission mode, even `bypassPermissions`: a guardrail, not a convention.
A non-fork **subagent** starts fresh: no chat history, no skills you invoked. It loads CLAUDE.md, preloads only skills in its `skills` field, and returns only its result.

sections.heading: CLAUDE.md: what every session should know
sections.body:
Every Claude Code session begins with a fresh context window. **CLAUDE.md** files carry your instructions across sessions: Claude reads them at the start of every session. A project `./CLAUDE.md` (or `./.claude/CLAUDE.md`) is shared with the team through version control; `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` holds personal preferences for all your projects.

**`/init`** analyzes your codebase and generates a starter file with the build commands, test instructions and conventions it discovers. If a CLAUDE.md already exists, it suggests improvements rather than overwriting it. Treat the result as a baseline to review, then refine it with what Claude wouldn't discover on its own.

A file that grows with every new instruction dilutes the rules that matter: longer files consume more context and reduce adherence. Target under 200 lines and, for each line, ask: would removing this cause Claude to make mistakes? If not, cut it. Keep build commands, conventions that differ from defaults and "always do X" rules. Move multi-step procedures and material needed only sometimes into **skills**, which load on demand. `@path` imports organize a long file but don't reduce its cost, because imported files also load at launch.

Claude treats CLAUDE.md as context, not enforced configuration, and if two instructions contradict each other it may pick one arbitrarily.
sections.example: An `/init` draft contains a file-by-file tour of `src/`, "write clean code", a 30-step release procedure and "run `make test-unit`, not `pytest`". Keep the test command, since Claude can't guess it. Cut the tour (Claude can read the code) and the self-evident advice. Move the release procedure into a skill that loads only when someone releases.

sections.heading: Rules files: guidance scoped to paths
sections.body:
For larger projects, split instructions into topic files in **`.claude/rules/`**, such as `testing.md` or `api-design.md`. A rule without `paths` frontmatter loads at launch with the same priority as `.claude/CLAUDE.md`.

Add a **`paths`** field with glob patterns and the rule becomes conditional: it loads only when Claude reads, writes or edits a matching file (a single-file read through Bash, such as `cat`, counts too). Guidance for one part of the codebase then stays out of context everywhere else.

- **CLAUDE.md:** broad project memory and universal constraints, such as build commands and project-wide conventions
- **Path-scoped rules:** narrow guidance for a file type or directory, such as API handler conventions under `src/api/`
- **Skills:** task-specific instructions that don't need to be in context all the time; they load when you invoke them or when Claude judges them relevant

Personal rules in `~/.claude/rules/` apply to every project on your machine and load before project rules. Neither set overrides the other: if a user rule and a project rule conflict, Claude may follow either one, so keep them consistent.
sections.example: `.claude/rules/api.md` starts with the frontmatter `paths: ["src/api/**/*.ts"]`, followed by "All API endpoints must include input validation" and "Use the standard error response format". Those rules enter context when Claude first opens a file under `src/api/`, not while it works on the frontend.

sections.heading: Hooks: guardrails at fixed lifecycle points
sections.body:
**Hooks** are your own shell commands (or HTTP, prompt or agent handlers) that Claude Code runs at specific points in its lifecycle. They give deterministic control: the action always happens, rather than relying on Claude to choose to do it.

- **SessionStart:** a session begins or resumes; a command's stdout is added to context, and the `compact` matcher re-injects context after compaction
- **UserPromptSubmit:** a prompt is submitted, before Claude processes it; can validate or block it
- **PreToolUse:** before a tool call executes; can block it
- **PostToolUse:** after a tool call succeeds; can't undo it
- **Notification:** Claude Code sends a notification, such as when it waits for input or permission
- **Stop:** Claude finishes responding; can send it back to work
- **SessionEnd:** the session terminates; useful for cleanup or logging

PreToolUse hooks fire before any permission-mode check, in every permission mode. A hook that denies a call blocks the tool even in `bypassPermissions` mode, so users can't bypass the policy by changing mode. A CLAUDE.md line saying "never edit the production config" is a **convention** Claude tries to follow; a PreToolUse hook that blocks edits to that path is a **guardrail** enforced on every matching call.
sections.example: In `.claude/settings.json`, register a `PreToolUse` hook with matcher `Edit|Write` that runs `.claude/hooks/protect-files.sh`. The script reads `tool_input.file_path` from stdin; if it matches `config/production.yaml`, it prints `Blocked: …` to stderr and exits 2. Claude Code blocks the edit before it runs and passes the message to Claude, so it can adjust its approach.

diagram.caption: A PreToolUse deny wins before the permission mode is even checked.

sections.heading: Subagents: delegating to an isolated context
sections.body:
A **subagent** is a specialized assistant Claude Code delegates tasks to. Each runs in its own context window with its own system prompt, tool access and permissions, does the work, and returns only its results, so verbose side work stays out of your main conversation.

A non-fork subagent starts fresh. It doesn't see your conversation history, the skills you've already invoked, or the files Claude has already read; it works from the delegation message Claude writes. It does load the CLAUDE.md hierarchy the main conversation loads (the built-in Explore and Plan agents skip it), but not the main conversation's auto memory. A decision that must reach a subagent belongs in CLAUDE.md or in the delegation prompt, not only in chat.

**Custom subagents** live in `.claude/agents/` (project; commit it to share) or `~/.claude/agents/` (personal). Each is YAML frontmatter, where only `name` and `description` are required, plus a markdown body that becomes its system prompt.

List skills in the **`skills`** field to inject their full content at startup. That field controls preloading, not access: without it, the subagent can still discover and invoke skills through the Skill tool. To stop it invoking skills, leave `Skill` out of `tools` or add it to `disallowedTools`.
sections.example: `.claude/agents/api-developer.md` sets `description: Implement API endpoints following team conventions` and `skills: [api-conventions, error-handling-patterns]`. Every run starts with both skills' full content, even if nobody invoked them in the main session, and the main conversation receives only the subagent's result.

sections.heading: The right mechanism for each concern
sections.body:
Durable context requires the right mechanism for each concern. Each feature has a recognizable trigger:

- Claude gets a convention or command wrong twice: add it to **CLAUDE.md**
- Guidance applies only to one language or directory: a **path-scoped rule**
- You keep pasting the same playbook or multi-step procedure into chat: capture it as a **skill**
- You want something to happen every time without asking: write a **hook**
- A side task floods your conversation with output you won't reference again: route it through a **subagent**

CLAUDE.md and rules files are context that Claude tries to follow, not enforcement. For anything that has to happen every time, or must never happen, use a hook.
sections.example: One 400-line CLAUDE.md, untangled: the build command stays in CLAUDE.md; API conventions move to `.claude/rules/api.md` with `paths`; the monthly release checklist becomes a skill; "run ESLint after every edit" becomes a PostToolUse hook; "never edit `config/production.yaml`" becomes a PreToolUse hook; log-heavy test runs go to a subagent.

title: Packaging workflows: skills, commands and plugins
summary: A skill packages a reusable workflow as a `SKILL.md` that Claude loads on demand. Claude Code, the API, the Agent SDK and Managed Agents each load skills their own way, so a skill that runs everywhere is something you design for. Give manual workflows an explicit entry point, and package a shareable setup as a plugin.
keyPoints: A skill is a `SKILL.md`: its frontmatter `description` says what it does and **when to use it** (the matching criterion); its body holds the steps.
Claude Code finds skills on disk; the API runs uploaded ones in the **code execution container**; the SDK loads them via `settingSources`; Managed Agents attach them.
Portable skills describe their trigger, don't assume local files, network or packages, and remember that a **fresh subagent doesn't see skills you've invoked**.
`disable-model-invocation: true` makes a skill manual-only; plugin skills are namespaced as **`/plugin-name:skill-name`**.
A **plugin** bundles skills, subagents, hooks and MCP servers into one installable unit, shared through a marketplace or deployed org-wide via managed settings.

sections.heading: Skills: reusable workflows loaded on demand
sections.body:
A **skill** is a reusable workflow packaged as a directory with a `SKILL.md` file. The file has two parts: YAML frontmatter between `---` markers that tells Claude when to use the skill, and a markdown body with the instructions Claude follows when it runs. Claude matches requests against the `description`, so it must say what the skill does **and** when to use it. Unlike a prompt, a skill loads on demand: until it's triggered, only its name and description sit in context.

In Claude Code, where you save a skill decides which sessions load it:

- **Personal:** `~/.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`, all your projects on this machine
- **Project:** `.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`, the repository's sessions; commit it so your team gets it too
- **Plugin:** `<plugin>/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`, wherever the plugin is enabled
- **Enterprise:** in the managed settings directory, for your whole organization

When two share a name, enterprise beats personal and personal beats project.
sections.example: A `deploy` skill's frontmatter holds `name: deploy` and `description: Deploy the application to production`. Its body lists the steps: run the test suite, build the application, push to the deployment target, verify the deployment succeeded. Saved in the repo's `.claude/skills/deploy/` and committed, it gives every teammate `/deploy`.

sections.heading: How a skill loads on each surface
sections.body:
The `SKILL.md` format is shared, but each surface gets a skill to Claude in its own way:

- **Claude Code:** discovered from `.claude/skills/` and `~/.claude/skills/` on the filesystem. Claude loads a skill when a request matches its description, or you invoke it by name as `/skill-name`.
- **Messages API:** you upload custom skills through the Skills API (they're shared workspace-wide) and name them by `skill_id` in the request's `container` parameter, with the code execution tool enabled. They run in that container, not in your application's environment.
- **Agent SDK:** skills are files on disk, discovered through the filesystem setting sources. Default options load user and project skills; set `settingSources` explicitly without `'project'` and project skills don't load. There's no programmatic API for registering a skill.
- **Claude Managed Agents:** the agent is an API resource naming the model, system prompt, tools, MCP servers and skills. Attach pre-built or uploaded skills in its `skills` array, or mount a GitHub repository whose root `.claude/skills/` is scanned at session start. Nothing is discovered on your machine.

Custom skills **don't sync** across surfaces, so set each one up separately on every surface that needs it.
sections.example: One `invoice-check` skill, three homes: committed under `.claude/skills/invoice-check/` for developers in Claude Code; uploaded once through the Skills API for the support app, which names its `skill_id` in `container`; and attached to a Managed Agent as `{"type": "custom", "skill_id": "skill_01…"}` in its `skills` array.

sections.heading: Three portability rules
sections.body:
A skill is portable, but "runs everywhere" is something you design for:

- **Write the description as the matching criterion.** Claude may choose from 100+ skills by name and description alone, so say what the skill does and the specific triggers for using it. Vague descriptions such as "Helps with documents" don't get picked.
- **Don't assume a local filesystem or local tools.** On the Claude API a skill has no network access and can't install packages at runtime; in Claude Code it has the same network access as any program on the user's computer. List the packages a skill needs, check they're available where it runs, and use forward-slash paths such as `scripts/validate.py`.
- **Remember that a fresh subagent starts without your skills.** A fresh subagent doesn't see the skills you've already invoked. To give a custom subagent a skill from its first turn, list it in the subagent's `skills` frontmatter, which injects the full content at startup. Without that, the subagent can still discover and invoke skills through the Skill tool, but it starts without them.
sections.example: A `quarterly-report` skill that runs `pip install` and calls an internal REST API works in Claude Code but fails on the Claude API, which has neither network access nor runtime installs. The portable version uses only pre-installed packages, keeps its logic in a bundled `scripts/build_report.py`, and has the app upload the input data with the Files API.

sections.heading: Explicit entry points: commands and manual-only skills
sections.body:
Some workflows should run only when a person asks. A **custom command** is a shortcut for a defined procedure that you run by typing `/name`. Custom commands have been merged into skills: `.claude/commands/deploy.md` and `.claude/skills/deploy/SKILL.md` both create `/deploy`, existing command files keep working, and if both exist the skill wins. Skills add a directory for supporting files and frontmatter that controls who invokes them.

To make a skill manual-only, set `disable-model-invocation: true`. You can still invoke it, Claude can't load it on its own, and its description isn't kept in context; the full skill loads when you invoke it. Use it for workflows with side effects, such as a deploy. The opposite setting, `user-invocable: false`, hides a skill from the `/` menu so only Claude invokes it.

Plugin skills are **namespaced** automatically: the plugin's name becomes the prefix. A `run-tests` skill in a plugin named `payments` runs as `/payments:run-tests`, so two plugins can each provide a skill with the same name without colliding.
sections.example: You convert a project's `/deploy` skill into a plugin named `release-tools`, so the copy runs as `/release-tools:deploy`. While the original still sits in `.claude/skills/`, `/deploy` and `/release-tools:deploy` both work. Once the plugin is confirmed, delete the original.

sections.heading: Plugins: the packaging layer
sections.body:
A **plugin** bundles skills, subagents, hooks and MCP servers (and other components) into one directory that Claude Code installs and loads as a unit, usually with a `.claude-plugin/plugin.json` manifest that names it. A **marketplace** is a catalog, a repository or directory with `.claude-plugin/marketplace.json`, listing plugins and where to fetch each: you add it once, then install plugins by name and receive updates. Administrators can deploy plugins organization-wide through **managed settings**: `extraKnownMarketplaces` registers the marketplace on every machine and `enabledPlugins` installs and enables the plugins, and users can't override them.

The packaging decision:

- **Skill:** a reusable procedure or knowledge Claude applies when relevant, standalone in `~/.claude/skills/` or the repo's `.claude/skills/`. Keep it standalone while it serves one project or only you.
- **Custom command:** a procedure that should run only when someone types `/name`; as a skill, set `disable-model-invocation: true`.
- **Plugin:** several components to share with teammates, install in several projects or publish as versioned releases.

An enabled plugin is part of every session: whatever Claude can invoke on its own puts its name and description in context, and the plugin runs as you.
sections.example: A platform team's `secure-dev` plugin holds a `threat-model` skill, a `security-reviewer` subagent, a hook that blocks edits to `.env` files and a scanning MCP server. They list it in the company marketplace, and managed settings register that marketplace and set `"secure-dev@company-tools": true` under `enabledPlugins`, so it loads on every developer's machine.

diagram.caption: A shareable setup: a marketplace lists the plugin, you install it, Claude Code loads its components.

title: Configuring MCP servers
summary: An MCP server packages tools, resources and prompts behind a standard protocol, so you don't write their schemas or code yourself. Adding one to Claude Code means two independent choices: the transport (how Claude Code talks to it) and the scope (who loads it). Permission rules, or the `mcp_toolset` on the API, then decide which of its tools may run.
keyPoints: Servers expose **tools** (the model calls them), **resources** (data fetched into context, via @ mentions) and **prompts** (vetted templates run as commands).
Transports: **stdio** for a local process, **HTTP** recommended for remote servers; **SSE** is deprecated.
Scopes: **local** (default; one project, `~/.claude.json`), **project** (`.mcp.json`, shared via git), **user** (all your projects); admins use managed config.
**Tool search** is on by default: only tool names and server instructions load at session start, so extra servers cost little context.
`mcp__server__tool` targets one tool and `mcp__server` the whole server; deny beats allow. On the API, `mcp_toolset` sets `enabled` per tool.

sections.heading: What an MCP server gives you
sections.body:
When you wire a tool directly into your application, you write its schema and run its code. An **MCP server** is a program that exposes capabilities to AI applications through standardized protocol interfaces instead, so a client such as Claude Code can use them without you writing either.

A server offers three building blocks:

- **Tools:** functions the model decides to call based on user requests, such as creating an issue.
- **Resources:** passive, read-only data (file contents, database schemas, API docs) that the application retrieves and provides to the model as context. Reach for one when you already know which data belongs in context, instead of waiting for the model to call a tool.
- **Prompts:** pre-built instruction templates that the user invokes explicitly, so a team can run one vetted template by name instead of everyone writing their own.
sections.example: In Claude Code, type `@` to reference a resource the way you reference a file: `Can you analyze @github:issue://123 and suggest a fix?` fetches the issue and attaches it. A server's prompts become commands: `/mcp__github__pr_review 456` runs the `pr_review` prompt with the argument 456, and its result is injected into the conversation.

sections.heading: Transport: how Claude Code talks to the server
sections.body:
The transport is the channel between the MCP client and the server. The same JSON-RPC message format is used on every transport; only the delivery changes.

- **stdio:** the server runs as a local process on your machine. Ideal for tools that need direct system access or custom scripts.
- **HTTP** (called Streamable HTTP in the MCP spec): the recommended option for remote servers and the most widely supported transport for cloud-based services. OAuth sign-in works with HTTP servers.
- **SSE:** an older transport, now deprecated. Use HTTP where available; some services still expose only an SSE endpoint.

On the Messages API, the MCP connector needs a server publicly exposed over HTTP; local stdio servers can't be connected to it directly.
sections.example: Remote: `claude mcp add --transport http notion https://mcp.notion.com/mcp`. Local: `claude mcp add --env AIRTABLE_API_KEY=YOUR_KEY --transport stdio airtable -- npx -y airtable-mcp-server`. Everything after the `--` is the command Claude Code runs to start the server; everything before it, including `--scope`, is Claude's own options.

sections.heading: Context cost and tool search
sections.body:
Every connected server contributes tool definitions, and loaded upfront they would fill the context window before you type anything. Claude Code handles this with **tool search**, on by default: only tool names and server instructions load at session start, and a tool's full definition arrives when Claude needs it. Adding servers then has minimal impact on your context window, and there's no fixed per-server tool cap.

- For a few tools Claude needs on every turn, set `alwaysLoad: true` on that server; each upfront tool costs context.
- Run `/context` to see what's using space, and disable servers you aren't using from `/mcp`.
- CLI tools such as `gh` are still more context-efficient, because they add no per-tool listing.

On the API, the same idea is `defer_loading` in an `mcp_toolset`, used with the tool search tool. A toolset can also carry a `cache_control` breakpoint, tying it into prompt caching from Section 2.

sections.heading: Scope: who loads the server
sections.body:
Scope controls which projects load a server and whether your team shares it:

- **Local** (the default): this project only, private to you, stored in `~/.claude.json` under the project's path. Good for experiments or credentials you keep out of version control.
- **Project:** written to `.mcp.json` at the repo root and checked in, so the whole team gets it. Claude Code asks for approval before using these servers in interactive sessions.
- **User:** all your projects, still private, also stored in `~/.claude.json`.
- **Managed:** administrators deploy or provide servers for everyone. A `managed-mcp.json` takes exclusive control; `managedMcpServers` adds servers alongside users' own.

Transport and scope are independent: a stdio server can be project-scoped and an HTTP server local. But the consequences depend on both. A shared `.mcp.json` reaches every teammate, so reference secrets and machine-specific paths as `${VAR}` instead of writing them in.
sections.example: `claude mcp add --transport http shared-server --scope project https://example.com/mcp` writes `{"mcpServers": {"shared-server": {"type": "http", "url": "https://example.com/mcp"}}}` to `.mcp.json`. A header such as `"Authorization": "Bearer ${API_KEY}"` keeps each developer's key out of the shared file.

diagram.caption: Same server defined in several places? The highest-precedence entry is used whole; fields aren't merged.

sections.heading: Permissions, mcp_toolset and the GitHub server
sections.body:
Connecting a server doesn't decide which of its tools may run. In Claude Code, permission rules name MCP tools by server and tool:

- `mcp__github` or `mcp__github__*` matches every tool on the `github` server.
- `mcp__github__create_issue` matches only that tool, so an allow rule on it skips the prompt for that one tool.
- Rules are evaluated deny, then ask, then allow, so a server-wide deny beats a tool-level allow.

Through the MCP connector on the API, the `mcp_toolset` does this job: every tool is enabled by default, and `default_config` plus per-tool `configs` give you an allowlist or a denylist.

The **GitHub MCP server** puts it together. It's remote, so it uses HTTP, and it authenticates with a GitHub personal access token passed as a header. Servers that use OAuth instead are signed in to from `/mcp`, with tokens stored securely and refreshed automatically.
sections.example: `claude mcp add --transport http github https://api.githubcopilot.com/mcp/ --header "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_GITHUB_PAT"` saves the server without validating the token, so check `/mcp`: an ✘ with a 401 means the credential was rejected. A rejected header you configured is reported as a failure; Claude Code doesn't fall back to OAuth.
